    62                  Proclamation 11069 of September 18, 2026
    63  
    64                  
    65  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant 
    66                  Workers
    67  
    68                  By the President of the United States of America
    69  
    70                  A Proclamation
    71  
    72                  On September 19, 2025, Proclamation 10973 (Restriction 
    73                  on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers) (2025 
    74                  Proclamation), was issued to address significant abuses 
    75                  of the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program. The restrictions 
    76                  enacted by the 2025 Proclamation have proven to be 
    77                  highly effective but the underlying conditions 
    78                  necessitating the restrictions persist. It is therefore 
    79                  in the interests of the United States to extend the 
    80                  2025 Proclamation for an additional 12 months, until 
    81                  12:00 a.m. eastern daylight time on September 21, 2027.
    82  
    83                  As explained in the 2025 Proclamation, the H-1B 
    84                  nonimmigrant visa program was created to bring 
    85                  temporary workers in high-skilled functions into the 
    86                  United States, but it has been exploited to replace, 
    87                  not supplement, American workers with lower-paid labor. 
    88                  Certain employers, including information technology 
    89                  (IT) staffing and outsourcing firms, have abused the 
    90                  system to suppress wages and displace American workers, 
    91                  and this has both harmed the labor market for American 
    92                  workers while also making it difficult to attract and 
    93                  retain the most highly skilled temporary workers. IT 
    94                  staffing and outsourcing firms were found to supply a 
    95                  large volume of entry-level temporary H-1B workers, 
    96                  generally at a much lower salary compared to full-time, 
    97                  traditional workers, and some of these firms later 
    98                  outsourced IT roles to cheap labor markets overseas. 
    99                  This has led to a proliferation of lower-paid foreign 
   100                  labor flooding the American labor market and making it 
   101                  difficult for American workers and recent graduates, 
   102                  especially in science, technology, engineering, and 
   103                  math (STEM) fields, to find employment.
   104  
   105                  To combat these abuses, the 2025 Proclamation set forth 
   106                  a restriction on entry of certain H-1B nonimmigrant 
   107                  workers, except for those petitions that were 
   108                  accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment, 
   109                  subject to very limited exceptions. The 2025 
   110                  Proclamation went into effect on September 21, 2025, 
   111                  and, since then, the $100,000 payment has been made for 
   112                  over 700 petitions.
   113  
   114                  Additionally, the 2025 Proclamation required initiation 
   115                  of rulemakings by the Department of Homeland Security 
   116                  (DHS) and the Department of Labor (DOL) to address 
   117                  systemic H-1B program concerns. On December 29, 2025, 
   118                  DHS published a final rule, titled Weighted Selection 
   119                  Process for Registrants and Petitioners Seeking to File 
   120                  Cap-Subject H-1B Petitions, 90 Fed. Reg. 60864 (DHS 
   121                  final rule), to address the policy goals consistent 
   122                  with section 4(b) of the 2025 Proclamation. Through 
   123                  this rule, DHS created and implemented a weighted 
   124                  selection process that prioritizes the allocation of 
   125                  visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens to 
   126                  better protect the wages, working conditions, and job 
   127                  opportunities for American workers. This policy better 
   128                  serves the intent of the H-1B statutory scheme, 
   129                  incentivizes employers to recruit temporary workers for 
   130                  roles at the highest pay and skill levels, and was in 
   131                  effect for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 H-1B cap season. 
   132                  On March 27, 2026, DOL published a notice of proposed 
   133                  rulemaking, titled Improving Wage Protections for the 
   134                  Temporary and Permanent Employment of Certain Foreign 
   135                  Nationals in the United States, 91 Fed. Reg. 15454,
   136  
   137  [[Page 60498]]
   138  
   139                  to address the policy goals consistent with section 
   140                  4(a) of the 2025 Proclamation. The DOL's analysis of 
   141                  labor condition application data found that the average 
   142                  wage actually paid to H-1B workers, and the prevailing 
   143                  wage assigned to their positions, both remain well 
   144                  below the average wage earned by comparable American 
   145                  workers. The rule, once finalized, will better align 
   146                  prevailing wage levels with wages paid to similarly 
   147                  employed and located American workers and will 
   148                  strengthen overall program integrity. Finally, my 
   149                  Administration continues to explore other complementary 
   150                  efforts that would, among other things, reform the H-1B 
   151                  program and assist with cost-recovery for immigration 
   152                  program administration.
   153  
   154                  Since the effective date of the 2025 Proclamation and 
   155                  subsequent promulgation of the DHS final rule, there 
   156                  have been several measurable impacts on the H-1B 
   157                  program, including a significant reduction in H-1B 
   158                  registrations filed by large IT outsourcing firms, with 
   159                  the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms reducing 
   160                  their combined H-1B registrations from 24,946 to 2,055, 
   161                  a 92 percent decrease. There has also been a large 
   162                  reduction in consular processing requests, which are 
   163                  used to bring workers into the United States, noting a 
   164                  nearly 97 percent decrease from the FY 2025 to FY 2027 
   165                  cap seasons. Finally, there has been a positive shift 
   166                  in FY 2027 H-1B registration and selection data toward 
   167                  higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, with 
   168                  registrations for beneficiaries with at least a U.S. 
   169                  Master's degree rising from 45.1 percent of total 
   170                  registrants for FY 2026 to 66.1 percent for FY 2027. 
   171                  Job offers with wages corresponding to the two highest 
   172                  wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3 percent of 
   173                  H-1B registration selections while those corresponding 
   174                  with the lowest wage level accounted for only 17.8 
   175                  percent. It is reasonable to conclude that the required 
   176                  $100,000 payment and newly implemented weighted 
   177                  selection process have had the combined effect of 
   178                  deterring low-wage and low-skilled recruitment while 
   179                  increasing access for high-skilled and high-wage 
   180                  workers, as intended by the 2025 Proclamation.
   181  
   182                  Although the 2025 Proclamation and subsequent 
   183                  rulemaking have had the desired effects, the underlying 
   184                  conditions precipitating their issuance persist and, 
   185                  without an extension of the 2025 Proclamation, it is 
   186                  highly likely that progress will halt and program abuse 
   187                  will resume, undermining American workers and posing a 
   188                  threat to the labor market that would be detrimental to 
   189                  the interests of the United States. The 2025 
   190                  Proclamation highlighted a number of concerns, 
   191                  including high unemployment rates for recent graduates, 
   192                  wage suppression, fraud, and national security threats. 
   193                  Currently, these issues continue to undermine our 
   194                  economy, with unemployment rates for recent college 
   195                  graduates standing at 5.7 percent as of June 2026, a 
   196                  marginal decrease from September 2025, when the rate 
   197                  was 5.8 percent. Underemployment for recent college 
   198                  graduates also continues to cause concern, having risen 
   199                  from 41.8 percent in September 2025 to 42 percent as of 
   200                  June 2026. Additionally, while DOL is actively in the 
   201                  process of promulgating a rule to restore integrity to 
   202                  the prevailing wage system, it will take a significant 
   203                  amount of time to correct and balance the labor market. 
   204                  Finally, while fraud and abuse continue to be 
   205                  identified and investigated, these are ongoing and 
   206                  pervasive concerns that require a sustained, 
   207                  comprehensive response reflected in the entry 
   208                  restriction imposed by the 2025 Proclamation.
   209  
   210                  A review of the 2025 Proclamation's impacts and other 
   211                  recent policy changes has shown significant measurable 
   212                  changes in H-1B filing patterns that demonstrate the 
   213                  effectiveness of the 2025 Proclamation and a need for 
   214                  its extension. An extension of the 2025 Proclamation 
   215                  will continue to protect the economic and national 
   216                  security interests of the United States, improve labor 
   217                  market access for American workers and graduates, and 
   218                  ensure that employers recruit only the most highly-
   219                  skilled and essential alien workers when needed in line 
   220                  with the original intent of the program. As a result, 
   221                  the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, the 
   222                  Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland 
   223                  Security have jointly recommended an extension of the 
   224                  2025 Proclamation.
   225  
   226  [[Page 60499]]
   227  
   228                  As a result of these reviews and considerations, I have 
   229                  decided to continue to impose the limitations set forth 
   230                  in Proclamation 10973 on the entry into the United 
   231                  States by certain nonimmigrant workers. Accordingly, by 
   232                  the authority vested in me as President by the 
   233                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
   234                  America, it is hereby ordered:
   235  
   236                  Section 1. Restriction on Entry. (a) Pursuant to 
   237                  sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and 
   238                  Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1182(f) and 1185(a)), 
   239                  the entry into the United States of aliens as 
   240                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   241                  occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA 
   242                  (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b)), is restricted, except 
   243                  for those aliens whose petitions are accompanied or 
   244                  supplemented by a payment of $100,000--subject to the 
   245                  exceptions set forth in subsection (c) of this section. 
   246                  This restriction shall expire, absent extension, 12 
   247                  months after the effective date of this proclamation, 
   248                  which shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   249                  September 21, 2026.
   250  
   251                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   252                  restrict decisions on petitions not accompanied by a 
   253                  $100,000 payment for H-1B specialty occupation workers 
   254                  under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA, who are 
   255                  currently outside the United States, for 12 months 
   256                  following the effective date of this proclamation as 
   257                  set forth in subsection (a) of this section.
   258                      (c) The restriction imposed pursuant to subsections 
   259                  (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any 
   260                  individual alien, all aliens working for a company, or 
   261                  all aliens working in an industry, if the Secretary of 
   262                  Homeland Security determines, in the Secretary's 
   263                  discretion, that the hiring of such aliens to be 
   264                  employed as H-1B specialty occupation workers is in the 
   265                  national interest and does not pose a threat to the 
   266                  security or welfare of the United States.
   267  
   268                  Sec. 2. Compliance. (a) Employers shall, prior to 
   269                  filing an H-1B petition on behalf of an alien outside 
   270                  the United States, obtain and retain documentation 
   271                  showing that the payment described in section 1 of this 
   272                  proclamation has been made.
   273  
   274                      (b) The Secretary of State shall verify receipt of 
   275                  payment of the amount described in section 1 of this 
   276                  proclamation during the H-1B visa petition process and 
   277                  shall approve only those visa applications for which 
   278                  the filing employer has made the payment described in 
   279                  section 1 of this proclamation.
   280                      (c) The Department of State and the Department of 
   281                  Homeland Security shall coordinate to take all 
   282                  necessary and appropriate action to implement this 
   283                  proclamation and to deny entry to the United States to 
   284                  any H-1B nonimmigrant for whom the prospective employer 
   285                  has not made the payment described in section 1 of this 
   286                  proclamation.
   287  
   288                  Sec. 3. Scope and Implementation of Restriction on 
   289                  Entry. (a) The restriction on entry pursuant to section 
   290                  1 of this proclamation shall apply only to aliens who 
   291                  enter or attempt to enter the United States after the 
   292                  effective date of this proclamation as set forth in 
   293                  section 1(a) of this proclamation. This restriction 
   294                  applies to aliens who must seek admission to the United 
   295                  States to effectuate the approval of a petition 
   296                  described in section 1 of this proclamation, including 
   297                  through consular notification, notification at a port 
   298                  of entry, pre-flight inspection, or pre-clearance.
   299  
   300                      (b) No later than 30 days following the completion 
   301                  of the H-1B lottery that immediately follows this 
   302                  proclamation, the Secretary of State, the Attorney 
   303                  General, the Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of 
   304                  Homeland Security shall jointly submit to the 
   305                  President, through the Assistant to the President and 
   306                  Homeland Security Advisor, a recommendation on whether 
   307                  an additional extension or renewal of the restriction 
   308                  on entry pursuant to section 1 of this proclamation is 
   309                  in the interests of the United States.
   310  
   311                  Sec. 4. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this 
   312                  proclamation shall be construed to impair or otherwise 
   313                  affect:
   314  
   315  (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or 
   316  the head thereof; or
   317  
   318  [[Page 60500]]
   319  
   320  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
   321  relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
   322  
   323                      (b) This proclamation shall be implemented 
   324                  consistent with applicable law and subject to the 
   325                  availability of appropriations.
   326                      (c) This proclamation is not intended to, and does 
   327                  not, create any right or benefit, substantive or 
   328                  procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any 
   329                  party against the United States, its departments, 
   330                  agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or 
   331                  agents, or any other person.
   332  
   333                  IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this 
   334                  eighteenth day of September, in the year of our Lord 
   335                  two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the 
   336                  United States of America the two hundred and fifty-
   337                  first.
   338                  
   339                  
   340                      (Presidential Sig.)

    23                  Executive Order 14431 of September 18, 2026
    24  
    25                  
    26  Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency 
    27                  Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B 
    28                  Nonimmigrant Visa Program
    29  
    30                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    31                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    32                  America, it is hereby ordered:
    33  
    34                  Section 1. Purpose. The H-1B nonimmigrant visa program 
    35                  was created to identify uniquely skilled and highly 
    36                  specialized foreign temporary workers to strategically 
    37                  supplement the United States economy. Instead, the 
    38                  program has been widely abused by certain employers, 
    39                  third-party placement groups, and outsourcing firms to 
    40                  undercut and displace the supply of skilled United 
    41                  States labor. The large-scale, systematic abuse of the 
    42                  H-1B program to obtain non-qualifying foreign labor has 
    43                  undermined the additive purpose of the program and 
    44                  harmed the wages, working conditions, and job 
    45                  opportunities of skilled American workers.
    46  
    47                  The abuse of cheaper H-1B labor places downward 
    48                  pressure on domestic pay. H-1B visa holders earn far 
    49                  less than comparable United States-born workers, 
    50                  despite the statutory mandate that H-1B workers be paid 
    51                  equally to their domestic peers, with the estimated 
    52                  wage gap starting at $9,000 and climbing as high as 
    53                  $20,000 in H-1B reliant industries. One company even 
    54                  warned its shareholders that restrictions on cheap H-1B 
    55                  labor could force the company to use ``local'' workers, 
    56                  which ``may only be available at higher wages.''
    57  
    58                  Many employers have laid off large numbers of highly 
    59                  skilled American workers, only to promptly hire large 
    60                  numbers of H-1B workers who are often lower-skilled and 
    61                  lower-paid. For instance, technology sector employers 
    62                  have collectively requested H-1B visas for hundreds of 
    63                  thousands of workers, yet have also laid off somewhere 
    64                  between 800,000 to 1.3 million American employees from 
    65                  2022 through 2026. Employers have even forced laid off 
    66                  American workers to train their foreign replacements.
    67  
    68                  Many jobs held by H-1B workers eventually leave the 
    69                  United States entirely. Employers with outsourcing 
    70                  business models use teams of H-1B visa holders to 
    71                  replace United States workers at third-party client 
    72                  businesses and liaise with other individuals working 
    73                  off-site from their country of origin. As soon as 
    74                  practicable, much of their own work is transferred 
    75                  offshore. In Fiscal Year 2026, the top six users of the 
    76                  H-1B program operating with this outsourcing business 
    77                  model accounted for over 25,000 H-1B cap registrations. 
    78                  One foreign country's foreign minister even publicly 
    79                  admitted that H-1B ``has become the outsourcing visa.''
    80  
    81                  The systematic and organized abuse of the H-1B program 
    82                  is also a national security threat. Domestic law 
    83                  enforcement agencies have investigated H-1B-reliant 
    84                  outsourcing firms for engaging in visa fraud, 
    85                  conspiracy to launder money, and other illicit 
    86                  activities to encourage foreign workers to come to the 
    87                  United States. Abuses of the H-1B program also present 
    88                  a national security threat by discouraging Americans 
    89                  from pursuing careers in science and technology, 
    90                  risking vital United States leadership in these fields.
    91  
    92                  Numerous executive departments and agencies (agencies) 
    93                  have flagged employers' large-scale, systematic abuse 
    94                  of the H-1B program to obtain lower-paid, lower-skilled 
    95                  labor from abroad. These ongoing Government probes 
    96                  continue to identify widespread fraud and noncompliance 
    97                  among H-1B
    98  
    99  [[Page 60502]]
   100  
   101                  employers, such as: displacing American workers or 
   102                  otherwise giving preference to alien workers; 
   103                  misrepresenting the duties, requirements, or working 
   104                  conditions of job opportunities to avoid hiring or 
   105                  training American workers, falsely qualify jobs as 
   106                  specialty occupations, or lower applicable wage 
   107                  requirements; and misrepresenting aliens' 
   108                  qualifications to perform specialty occupations by 
   109                  submitting questionable foreign degrees from diploma 
   110                  mills as support for their H-1B visa applications. The 
   111                  pervasiveness of these violations and the persistence 
   112                  of the violators confirm that more needs to be done to 
   113                  preserve the H-1B program's integrity.
   114  
   115                  I have determined that continued efforts must be made 
   116                  to protect and prioritize the American workforce. It is 
   117                  therefore the policy of the United States that all 
   118                  relevant agencies shall implement appropriate measures 
   119                  to protect American workers from abuse of the H-1B 
   120                  program and ensure that the program serves the national 
   121                  interest.
   122  
   123                  Sec. 2. Interagency Coordination. When processing 
   124                  petitions, labor condition applications, and visas for 
   125                  the entry into the United States of aliens as 
   126                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   127                  occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the 
   128                  Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 
   129                  1101(a)), the Secretary of State, the Secretary of 
   130                  Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   131                  coordinate and consult with the Secretary of Commerce, 
   132                  the Secretary of Education, and the Administrator of 
   133                  the Small Business Administration to ensure the 
   134                  compliance of such petitions, applications, and visas 
   135                  with statutory requirements, including those in 
   136                  sections 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b), 212(n), 214(i), and 274B 
   137                  of the INA. The Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of 
   138                  Education, and the Administrator of the Small Business 
   139                  Administration shall provide any relevant wage, 
   140                  employment, academic, industrial, or other economic 
   141                  information.
   142  
   143                  Sec. 3. Consideration of Applications, Petitions, and 
   144                  Visas. (a) Consistent with sections 
   145                  101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b), 212(n), 214(i), 215(a), and 274B 
   146                  of the INA, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of 
   147                  Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   148                  take into account in any labor condition application, 
   149                  petition, visa, and entry of aliens entering or 
   150                  attempting to enter the United States as H-1B 
   151                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   152                  occupation whether the employer sponsor directly or 
   153                  indirectly engaged in layoffs within the previous year 
   154                  or plans future layoffs that negatively affect the 
   155                  employment of similarly situated United States workers.
   156  
   157                      (b) Within 30 days of the date of this order, the 
   158                  Secretary of Labor, through the Administrator of the 
   159                  Wage and Hour Division, shall begin reviewing data 
   160                  related to previously submitted labor condition 
   161                  applications to determine whether further action

Abstract:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is amending the regulations concerning the 9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee for certain H-1B and L-1 Visas (9-11 Biometric Fee). The regulatory changes correct DHS's interpretation of statutory language to require that covered employers submit the 9-11 Biometric Fee for all extension of status petitions, regardless of whether the related fraud prevention and detection fee applies, which includes extension of status petitions that do not involve a change of employer. The 9-11 Biometric Fee continues to apply unchanged to petitions seeking an initial grant of status. The changes also help DHS comply with its congressional mandate to implement a biometric entry-exit system.

   144      On December 18, 2015, Congress established the 9-11 Biometric Fee.

   148  Biometric Fee after the 2010 Supplemental Fee expired. The 9-11 
   149  Biometric Fee doubled the amount of the 2010 Supplemental Fee, 
   150  providing ``the combined filing fee and fraud prevention and detection 
   151  fee [ . . . ] shall be increased by $4,500 [or $4,000]''. Id.
   152  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   153  
   154      \4\ The 9-11 Biometric Fee is a fee related to petitions for H-
   155  1B and L-1 classification and is discussed in those terms in this 
   156  rulemaking. Although not all those seeking H-1B and L-1 
   157  classification are required to obtain a visa, the headings in the 
   158  statute refer to temporary fee increases for H-1B and L-1 visas, and 
   159  consequently the headings in the implementing regulations refer to 
   160  fees for H-1B and L-1 visas. Accordingly, the subject heading of 
   161  this document and the regulatory headings also refer to fees for H-
   162  1B and L-1 visas.
   163  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   164  
   165      The statutory language in Public Law 114-113 establishing the 9-11 
   166  Biometric Fee is similar to that of Public Law 111-230.\5\ However, 
   167  Public Law 114-113 has two important distinctions, beyond the increased 
   168  fee amounts. First, Congress added the word ``combined,'' clarifying 
   169  that the fee increase served as a single fee increase to the filing 
   170  fee. Sec. 402(g), Public Law 114-113. Second, with respect to the types 
   171  of petitions for which the fees must be submitted, Congress inserted 
   172  the phrase ``including an application \6\ for an extension of such 
   173  status.'' Id. This addition clarified that the 9-11 Biometric Fee is 
   174  required for both petitions seeking an initial grant of status and 
   175  extension of status petitions.

   179  fraud prevention and detection fee required to be submitted with an

   181  application for an extension of such status, shall be increased by 
   182  $4,500 . . .'') with Public Law 114-113 (``the filing fee and fraud 
   183  prevention and detection fee required to be submitted with an

Document number:   2026-18631
Title:             Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period
Type:              Proposed Rule
Action:            Notice of proposed rulemaking.
Agencies:          Homeland Security Department
Citation:          91 FR 57807
Pages:             57807-57828 (22 pages)
Published:         2026-09-11
Comments close:    2026-11-10
Dates:             Written comments on the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) must be submitted on or before November 10, 2026. The electronic Federal Docket Management System will accept comments before midnight eastern time at the end of that day.
Docket:            CIS No. 2858-26; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364
RIN:               1615-AD22
CFR affected:      8 CFR 204, 8 CFR 214
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Adoption and foster care, Aliens, Cultural exchange programs, Employment, Foreign officials, Health professions, Immigration, Reporting and recordkeeping requirements, Students
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/11/2026-18631/eliminating-the-discretionary-60-day-grace-period
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-09-11/pdf/2026-18631.pdf

Abstract:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposes to remove regulations at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) to restore its previous and long- standing policy of not providing aliens in certain nonimmigrant classifications (and their dependents) with an up to 60-day grace period upon cessation of employment prior to the expiration of the alien's authorized period of stay. This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien's nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden.

Use `toc`, `grep` or `text` with this document number to read the full text.

  1664      The proposed rule would also establish a fee of $30,000 per F-1 
  1665  nonimmigrant student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that make any 
  1666  subsequent OPT recommendation for an F-1 nonimmigrant student who has 
  1667  previously participated in OPT and has previously paid the initial OPT

  1669  subsequent $30,000 fee would apply to any type of OPT that an F-1

  1672  post-completion OPT, or STEM OPT extension). Id. The OPT fee is not 
  1673  triggered by a change in employer but rather a school's decision to 
  1674  recommend a student for any type of OPT. For example, if an F-1 
  1675  nonimmigrant student obtains a DSO recommendation for pre-completion 
  1676  OPT and completes the training, they would need to obtain a subsequent 
  1677  DSO recommendation for post-completion OPT, regardless of whether the 
  1678  employer is the same for post-completion OPT and pre-completion OPT. In

  1681  As with the initial OPT fee, the subsequent OPT fee would need to be 
  1682  paid for the F-1 nonimmigrant student prior to the DSO entering the OPT 
  1683  recommendation in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii). 
  1684  Additionally, USCIS would not grant employment authorization to any 
  1685  student prior to payment of the applicable OPT fee for the student. See 
  1686  proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii).
  1687      The proposed rule reiterates that the schools must pay the 
  1688  applicable OPT fees prior to the DSO entering the OPT recommendation 
  1689  for an F-1 nonimmigrant student in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 
  1690  214.2(f)(11)(i)-(ii), 214.13(i). A DSO may not enter the OPT 
  1691  recommendation in SEVIS if the OPT fee has not yet been paid. The 
  1692  proposed rule requires the DSO to confirm that the school has paid the 
  1693  applicable OPT fee prior to updating SEVIS with the DSO's 
  1694  recommendation and before the student can apply to USCIS for employment 
  1695  authorization. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)(B). The DSO would 
  1696  need to provide the F-1 nonimmigrant student with a new I-20 with the

  1761  rulemaking along with the statutory authority to take such action.\119 
  1762  \In proposing this rule, DHS considered the following: fraud concerns; 
  1763  the need to ensure that institutions are remaining diligent in their 
  1764  oversight of F-1 nonimmigrant students such that F-1 nonimmigrant 
  1765  students are engaging in legitimate OPT directly related to the F-1 
  1766  nonimmigrant student's major area of study; protecting the interests of 
  1767  U.S.
  1768  
  1769  [[Page 64578]]
  1770  
  1771  workers; and the benefits of providing clarity on the requirements of 
  1772  OPT for F-1 nonimmigrant students, educational institutions, and 
  1773  employers. DHS has determined that these issues outweigh any 
  1774  stakeholder's reliance interest. The national interest in protecting 
  1775  American workers and program integrity far outweighs any reliance 
  1776  interests of foreign students, employers (including state and 
  1777  government employers), or educational institutions. The F-1 visa was 
  1778  never intended to provide a pathway to employment in the United States.
  1779  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1780  
  1781      \119\ For a full discussion on Transition Period and Effective 
  1782  Date, see section V.C above.
  1783  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1784  
  1785      Throughout the INA, Congress has drawn clear distinctions between 
  1786  different classes of aliens and the benefits to which they are 
  1787  entitled.\120 \The F-1 visa classification is for nonimmigrants who 
  1788  intend to come to the United States ``solely for the purpose of 
  1789  pursuing . . . a course of study'' and not an ancillary purpose, such 
  1790  as seeking employment.\121\ Additionally, the F-1 nonimmigrant 
  1791  classification is for aliens who have no intention of abandoning their 
  1792  foreign residence.\122\ A number of factors play a role in an F-1 
  1793  nonimmigrant student selecting an institution and course of study, 
  1794  including, but not limited to: geographic location, school rankings and 
  1795  prestige, program availability, campus culture, housing, sporting 
  1796  programs, and tuition costs. While DHS considered that the opportunity 
  1797  an institution provides for OPT may be one of many factors, it is 
  1798  speculative to assume that the ability to participate in OPT, which 
  1799  requires authorization by a SEVP-certified educational institution and 
  1800  the U.S. Government and is by law temporary in nature, is the sole 
  1801  reason a student decided to enter the United States on a F-1 
  1802  classification. In fact, only about 20 percent of F-1 nonimmigrants 
  1803  participated in OPT in 2024 out of the 1.4 million F-1 nonimmigrants in 
  1804  the higher education system, which demonstrates that the vast majority 
  1805  of F-1 nonimmigrants choose to study in the United States for reasons 
  1806  other than to pursue work through OPT.\123\ Regardless of whether F-1 
  1807  nonimmigrants participate in OPT, which is by definition not required 
  1808  to obtain their degree, they realize enormous benefits in studying at 
  1809  the prestigious institutions America offers and obtaining degrees from 
  1810  these institutions. Moreover, F-1 nonimmigrants may pursue appropriate 
  1811  channels to obtain employment in the United States other than the OPT, 
  1812  such as through the H-1B visa following graduation or on-campus or off-
  1813  campus employment during the program of study. Accordingly, DHS 
  1814  believes that any potential reliance interests on the part of 
  1815  prospective F-1 students and current F-1 students who have not yet 
  1816  received a DSO recommendation for OPT is outweighed by the benefits 
  1817  described above.\124\ In addition, DHS is proposing to apply this rule 
  1818  to those F-1 nonimmigrant students who receive a DSO recommendation for 
  1819  OPT that is dated on or after the effective date of the final rule. DHS 
  1820  believes this should address any potential reliance interests of 
  1821  students who have applied for OPT employment authorization before the 
  1822  effective date.

Action:            Final rule.
Agencies:          Homeland Security Department
Citation:          91 FR 65306
Pages:             65306-65368 (63 pages)
Published:         2026-10-14
Effective:         2026-10-14
Dates:             This final rule is effective on October 14, 2026.
Docket:            CIS No. 2859-26; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2025-0271
RIN:               1615-AD05
CFR affected:      8 CFR 274
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Aliens, Cultural exchange programs, Employment, Penalties, Reporting and recordkeeping requirements, Students
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/14/2026-20955/removal-of-automatic-extensions-for-certain-employment-authorization-documents
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-14/pdf/2026-20955.pdf

Abstract:
On October 30, 2025, DHS published an interim final rule (IFR) that amended DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I- 766 or EADs) for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization categories. This final rule responds to comments received on the IFR and reaffirms and finalizes the provisions of the IFR. Ending the automatic extension of EADs enhances benefit integrity and prioritizes the proper vetting and screening of aliens before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD.

Use `toc`, `grep` or `text` with this document number to read the full text.

  8440  [[Page 45042]]
  8441  
  8442  year, including discovery of new academic interests, poor academic fit, 
  8443  financial constraints, family circumstances, safety concerns, 
  8444  discriminatory treatment, school closures, program eliminations, and 
  8445  the need for additional language training. Commenters also expressed 
  8446  concern that the transfer restriction would particularly impact English 
  8447  language programs and community colleges, potentially increasing costs 
  8448  and time to degree completion. Clarification was sought about when 
  8449  transfers would be allowed for F-1 students.
  8450      Response: Undergraduate students seeking to transfer to another 
  8451  school or change their educational objectives during their first year 
  8452  of study still retain flexibility in having their cases reviewed by 
  8453  DHS, which may then authorize the change in educational objective or 
  8454  school transfer if an exception is warranted. Transfers to other 
  8455  schools or changing majors after the first year of study is allowed at 
  8456  the undergraduate level, including for students who do not meet certain 
  8457  requirements to progress within their program and change majors. Any 
  8458  graduate student that fails out of the program will need to return 
  8459  home.
  8460      This particular change seeks to address significant costs incurred 
  8461  by universities when working with potential F-1 students who then 
  8462  transfer to less expensive schools upon arrival in the United States. 
  8463  This provision will provide more stability in the admission process and 
  8464  still provides the students with the ability to explore coursework and 
  8465  majors during the first year. Most undergraduate students take similar 
  8466  classes in their first year; therefore, the majority of the commenters' 
  8467  objections about changing degrees in the first year are not a concern 
  8468  under this new framework.
  8469  f. Program Changes for Graduate Students
  8470      Comments: Commenters stated that changes to graduate programs do 
  8471  not account for actual experiences of students. The majority of 
  8472  commenters expressed opposition to the proposed rule's prohibition on 
  8473  F-1 graduate students changing programs or educational objectives 
  8474  during their program of study. Commenters expressed particular concern 
  8475  about the impact on Ph.D. students, remarking that the proposed 
  8476  restrictions demonstrate a lack of understanding about the nature of 
  8477  graduate education, which often involves interdisciplinary work and 
  8478  evolving research interests.
  8479      Commenters stated that the rule would disrupt common practices in 
  8480  graduate education, including master's students being promoted to Ph.D. 
  8481  programs midway through their studies, Ph.D. students receiving 
  8482  master's degrees enroute to their doctorate, and students pursuing dual 
  8483  degrees at the graduate level. Another commenter expressed the proposed 
  8484  rule would eliminate the ``master-out'' option for Ph.D. students who 
  8485  are awarded a master's degree when they cannot finish, and harm 
  8486  ``academic mobility'' for second master's degrees and master's-out 
  8487  pathways. Commenters clarified that graduate school, particularly at 
  8488  the doctoral level, is not a fixed, linear path, and intellectual 
  8489  discovery often leads students to pivot to related fields. Commenters 
  8490  stated that the rule would punish academic growth by causing students 
  8491  to abandon years of work rather than transition programs. Many 
  8492  commenters expressed concern with the proposed rule's different 
  8493  provisions for graduate students compared to undergraduate students, 
  8494  noting that the proposed rule lacks explanation or rationale for these 
  8495  distinctions. One commenter reported extenuating and uncontrollable 
  8496  circumstances may cause a graduate student to transfer programs or 
  8497  institutions, while another commenter thought the proposed rule would 
  8498  punish students for issues beyond their control by locking students 
  8499  into a major their first year and by requiring graduate students to 
  8500  remain in their program. Another commenter stated that the proposed 
  8501  rule would make Ph.D. enrollment riskier and would leave open teaching 
  8502  assistant and research positions that are dependent on foreign 
  8503  students.
  8504      Commenters provided numerous reasons why graduate students might 
  8505  need to change programs, including refined research direction, changes 
  8506  in advisors, moves from master's to doctoral programs, suggestions from 
  8507  faculty members, personal or academic circumstances, and changes in 
  8508  research funding. Commenters emphasized the critical relationship 
  8509  between graduate students and their faculty advisors, explaining that 
  8510  students often choose specific institutions because of faculty members 
  8511  whose research aligns with their interests, reasoning that when faculty 
  8512  members relocate to another university, graduate students may need to 
  8513  transfer to continue working with their chosen mentors and maintain 
  8514  access to specialized research facilities. Commenters noted that 
  8515  research funding is often tied to specific faculty members, requiring 
  8516  students to follow their advisors to maintain financial support.
  8517      Commenters urged DHS to reconsider its restrictions on graduate 
  8518  students seeking to transfer or change educational objectives, with 
  8519  specific requests to allow Ph.D. students the option to transfer, 
  8520  particularly in cases involving academic or financial necessity. If DHS 
  8521  proceeds with finalizing the rule, commenters suggested establishing 
  8522  exceptions, such as allowing students to transfer to continue 
  8523  mentorship with their advisor, and proposed simplifying procedures for 
  8524  program extensions and transfers, especially at the graduate level. 
  8525  Commenters asked what happens after the 240-day authorized stay ends 
  8526  while an application is pending, the earliest filing date for 
  8527  applications, and how Ph.D. students whose programs exceed four years 
  8528  would justify extensions.
  8529      Commenters noted the rule could prevent individuals who completed a 
  8530  Ph.D. from later enrolling in a U.S. MD program or vice versa, despite 
  8531  these degrees preparing students for distinct career paths. Commenters 
  8532  expressed concern about uncertainty for medical residents on F-1 visas 
  8533  regarding whether residency would be considered a higher education 
  8534  level than medical school, potential barriers to changing disciplines 
  8535  during residency, and disruptions to transitions between PharmD 
  8536  programs or movement from PharmD to research-focused graduate programs.
  8537      Relatedly, a few commenters noted that the changes would prohibit 
  8538  students from pursuing a second master's degree which could hamper 
  8539  their ability to shift careers and add interdisciplinary training. One 
  8540  commenter pursuing a second STEM master's degree also expressed concern 
  8541  for the uncertainty surrounding using OPT after a second master's 
  8542  degree and stated that this might direct students away from the United 
  8543  States. Another commenter spoke about how the inability to pursue a 
  8544  second master's degree may hamper a student from ``applied, industry-
  8545  ready training.''
  8546      Response: DHS acknowledges that students may seek to engage in 
  8547  programs simultaneously at a lower level or obtain multiple degrees, at 
  8548  differing levels, throughout the course of their time in the United 
  8549  States. Students will be able to continue earning such credentials 
  8550  while also making progress in the degree program for which they have 
  8551  been issued a Form I-20. For example, a student issued a Form I-20 for 
  8552  a Ph.D. program as their primary academic objective could obtain a 
  8553  master's degree incidental to
  8554  
  8555  [[Page 45043]]
  8556  
  8557  status while progressing toward completion of the Ph.D. program.
  8558      DHS generally relies on NCES' definition of educational levels, 
  8559  which provides a structure for determining whether a nonimmigrant 
  8560  student's program of study reflects upward academic progression. The 
  8561  list of educational levels that schools use to update their Form I-17, 
  8562  ``Petition for Approval of School for Attendance by Nonimmigrant 
  8563  student,'' is available at https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/sevis-help-hub/school-records/school-certification/form-i-17-listing-of-available-degrees. This list contains the following educational levels: 1. 
  8564  Primary and Secondary Education; 2. ELT; 3. Post-secondary 
  8565  Certificates/Non-Degree; 4. Associate; 5. Bachelor; 6. Master; 7. 
  8566  Doctorate. DHS may provide updated guidance on educational levels to 
  8567  ensure consistency across components and with ED.
  8568      DHS appreciates commenters' concerns about the rule's effect on 
  8569  academic growth of students. DHS recognizes academic pathways can be 
  8570  complex and that students may pursue multiple degrees or transition 
  8571  programs, including from undergraduate to graduate studies. The 
  8572  Department does not intend to discourage academic advancement or 
  8573  require students to abandon years of work.
  8574      DHS also recognizes the different approaches for undergraduate 
  8575  students and graduate students. This rule aims to balance program 
  8576  integrity and national security with the need to support legitimate 
  8577  educational pursuits. DHS believes differing approaches for 
  8578  undergraduate and graduate students are appropriate given the 
  8579  difference in the general ages of the students, a graduate student's 
  8580  previous opportunities to explore academic interests prior to entering 
  8581  graduate school, and a focus on more specific degree programs at the 
  8582  graduate level. DHS maintains it is appropriate to prohibit an F-1 
  8583  student at the graduate degree level or above from changing educational 
  8584  objectives at any point during their program of study for the reasons 
  8585  outlined above. However, DHS recognizes that extenuating circumstances, 
  8586  such as a school closure or a school's prolonged inability to hold in-
  8587  person classes due to a natural disaster, may prevent a graduate 
  8588  student from being able to continue their studies unless the student 
  8589  transfers to another SEVP-certified institution. The NPRM proposed 
  8590  prohibiting an F-1 student at the graduate level from transferring, 
  8591  without exception. DHS agrees with commenters that these situations may 
  8592  be outside the students' control and, taking this into consideration, 
  8593  DHS has amended the regulatory text to allow SEVP to authorize an 
  8594  exception to this transfer prohibition in extenuating circumstances. 
  8595  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C), and 8 CFR 
  8596  214.2(f)(8)(i)(D). For the purposes of this rule, ``extenuating 
  8597  circumstances'' for a transfer are rare, exceptional events beyond the 
  8598  control of the school and the affected students that prevent an SEVP-
  8599  certified school from continuing to provide the student's approved 
  8600  course of study, such as a permanent or extended school closure, a 
  8601  school merger that eliminates the student's program, a loss of 
  8602  necessary authorization for the school to enroll F-1 students, or the 
  8603  school's prolonged inability to deliver required instruction due to a 
  8604  natural disaster or comparable emergency. In such circumstances, SEVP 
  8605  may, in its discretion and in coordination with the impacted SEVP-

 15885  F. Requirements for Admission, Extension, and Maintenance of Status of 
 15886  F Nonimmigrants
 15887  
 15888      Under this final rule, as outlined in the proposed rule, DHS has 
 15889  changed the regulations that provide the framework for admission, 
 15890  extension, and maintenance of status for F nonimmigrants. These changes 
 15891  will eliminate D/S, require students to file an EOS if requesting to 
 15892  remain in the United States beyond the period of their admission, and 
 15893  clarify terms to ensure that the activities an F nonimmigrant has 
 15894  engaged in are consistent with those of a bona fide student.
 15895  1. Admission for a Fixed Time Period
 15896      In the NPRM, DHS proposed striking the previous regulation that 
 15897  allows F nonimmigrants to be admitted for D/S while also proposing to 
 15898  replace it with a provision allowing F nonimmigrants to be granted 
 15899  status for the length of their program, not to exceed 4 years. See 
 15900  proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) and (f)(7)(vi). This is retained in the 
 15901  final rule with additional clarity added to new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i). 
 15902  More specifically, that paragraph references instances when additional 
 15903  time may be granted to an F-1 student by adding language to reference 
 15904  the completion of their program of study, as described in paragraphs 
 15905  (f)(7) and (f)(8)(iv) of that section and the beginning of a new 
 15906  program of study, as described in paragraphs (f)(5)(ii)(D) and (f)(7) 
 15907  of that section.
 15908      Second, the NPRM proposed retaining in the regulations the 
 15909  statutory limitation that restricts public high school students to an 
 15910  aggregate of 12 months of study at any public high school(s) while also 
 15911  clarifying that the 12-month aggregate period includes any school 
 15912  breaks and annual vacations. This is retained in the final rule with 
 15913  clarification that a public high school may also include a charter 
 15914  school or other similar school funded by U.S. taxpayers. See new 8 CFR 
 15915  214.2(f)(5)(i)(C). Current requirements, including paying the full cost 
 15916  of education, also remain in place.
 15917      Third, F-1 students who are applying to attend an approved private 
 15918  elementary or middle school or private academic high school will 
 15919  continue to be covered by the provisions of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i)(E). 
 15920  These provisions require the DSO to certify a minimum number of class 
 15921  hours per week prescribed by the school for normal progress toward 
 15922  graduation. See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i)(E). However, like all other F-1 
 15923  students, they will be subject to the 4-year maximum period of 
 15924  admission, and they will need to apply for an EOS with DHS if staying 
 15925  beyond this period. This is retained in the final rule. See new 8 CFR 
 15926  214.2(f)(7)(vi).
 15927      Fourth, DHS proposed exempting part-time border commuter students
 15928  
 15929  [[Page 45103]]
 15930  
 15931  from the general length of admission provisions. The regulations at 8 
 15932  CFR 214.2(f)(18) would continue to govern these border commuter 
 15933  students, including that DHS continue to admit them for a fixed time 
 15934  period. This is retained in the final rule. See new 8 CFR 
 15935  214.2(f)(5)(i)(B).
 15936      Fifth, F-1 students in a language training program will be 
 15937  restricted to an aggregate of 24 months of language study, which will 
 15938  include breaks and an annual vacation. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A). 
 15939  This limitation is a way to prevent abuse of the F-1 program. Public 
 15940  Law 111-306, enacted on December 14, 2010, and effective since 2011, 
 15941  requires language training schools enrolling F-1 students to be 
 15942  accredited by an accrediting agency recognized by the ED. DHS has found 
 15943  students enrolling in lengthy periods of language training, in some 
 15944  cases for more than two decades.\307\ DHS has also identified students 
 15945  who enrolled in language training programs despite previously being 
 15946  enrolled in or completing undergraduate and graduate programs requiring 
 15947  English language proficiency.\308\ Unlike degree programs that 
 15948  typically have prescribed course completion requirements, there are no 
 15949  nationally-recognized, standard completion requirements for language 
 15950  training programs and students are able to enroll in language training 
 15951  programs for lengthy periods of time. The lengthy enrollment in a 
 15952  language program, including enrollment in language courses for long 
 15953  periods subsequent to completion of a program of study that requires 
 15954  proficiency in English, raises concerns about whether the F-1 
 15955  nonimmigrants meet the statutory definition of a bona fide student with 
 15956  the intent of entering the United States for temporary study.\309\ 
 15957  Therefore, there is a 24-month aggregate limit for F-1 students to 
 15958  participate in a language training program, as it will provide a 
 15959  reasonable period of time for students to attain proficiency while 
 15960  mitigating DHS's concerns about the integrity of the program. This 
 15961  timeframe generally comports with the amount of time needed to gain the 
 15962  highest level of English proficiency under the Cambridge English 
 15963  Exam.\310\ This is retained in the final rule.

 15965  
 15966      \307\ For example, one student has been enrolled in ELT programs 
 15967  at nine different schools since January 3, 2003. This student is 
 15968  active in SEVIS, reportedly studying English full time as of May 7, 
 15969  2025--accounting for more than 22 years of language training. The 
 15970  student's most recent school issued a program extension changing the 
 15971  student's program end date from January 2, 2025, to January 2, 2026. 
 15972  The school input the following reason for the extension: ``Student 
 15973  pursuing advanced level linguistic studies.'' The school's 2025 
 15974  catalog contains no references to linguistic studies--advanced or 
 15975  otherwise--and indicates the school offers general English academic 
 15976  preparation, TOEFL preparation, and business English courses. DHS 
 15977  analysis of data in SEVIS and valid as of May 7, 2025.
 15978      \308\ SEVIS Records show that for example a student who entered 
 15979  the country in 2005 studied English and then between January 2011 
 15980  and December 2024, he enrolled in a bachelor's program in Biology/
 15981  Biological Sciences, a master's program in Biotechnology, and a 
 15982  second master's program in Bioinformatics. He also engaged in post-
 15983  completion OPT and two periods of STEM OPT. Each of his Forms I-20 
 15984  indicated the academic programs required English proficiency, and 
 15985  the student had English proficiency. However, in January 2025, the 
 15986  student transferred to a language training school and remains active 
 15987  in SEVIS reportedly engaged in ELT as of May 7, 2025. DHS found at 
 15988  least 20 similar examples. DHS analysis of data in SEVIS and valid 
 15989  as of May 7, 2025.
 15990      \309\ See INA 101(a)(15)(F).
 15991      \310\ See Cambridge English, supra note 195.

 15994      Sixth, DHS proposed students with pending employment authorization 
 15995  applications who are admitted based on the DSO's recommended employment 
 15996  end date for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT specified on their Form I-
 15997  20, with a notice issued by USCIS indicating receipt of the Application

 15999  completion OPT or STEM OPT, and who cease employment authorized 
 16000  pursuant to a post-completion OPT- or STEM OPT-based EAD that expires 
 16001  before the alien's fixed date of admission as noted on their Arrival/
 16002  Departure Record (Form I-94 or successor form), be considered to be in

 16004  expiration noted on their EAD until the fixed date of admission as 
 16005  noted on their I-94 (unless the student violates the terms of the 
 16006  authorized stay). This is retained in the final rule. See new 8 CFR 
 16007  214.2(f)(5)(i)(D).
 16008      Seventh, the authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents cannot 
 16009  exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 student. DHS 
 16010  proposed adding this requirement and retains this proposal in the final 
 16011  rule. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E).
 16012  2. Changes in Educational Objectives
 16013      Prior to the implementation of this final rule, all F-1 students 
 16014  who change from one educational level to another or pursue multiple 
 16015  degrees in the same educational level are considered to be maintaining 
 16016  status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii). DHS has observed that some 
 16017  students continuously enroll in different programs at the same degree 
 16018  level, such as by pursuing multiple associate, master's, undergraduate, 
 16019  bachelor's, or certificate programs. Alternatively, some students 
 16020  change to a lower educational level, such as completing a master's 
 16021  degree and then changing to an associate's program or an ELT 
 16022  program.\311\ This has enabled some aliens to remain in the United 
 16023  States for lengthy periods of time in F-1 student status, raising 
 16024  concerns about the temporary nature of their stay. In 2024, DHS 
 16025  identified nearly 77,000 F-1 students who have spent more than 10 years 
 16026  in student status since SEVIS was implemented in 2003.\312\ This 
 16027  includes individuals who enrolled in programs at the same educational 
 16028  level as many as 19 times, as well as students who completed graduate 
 16029  programs and then enrolled in undergraduate programs, including 
 16030  associate's degrees.\313\
 16031  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16032  
 16033      \311\ Id.
 16034      \312\ DHS analysis of data in SEVIS and valid as of Mar. 17, 
 16035  2025.
 16036      \313\ Id.
 16037  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16038  
 16039      DHS has also observed a pattern of students immediately 
 16040  transferring schools or changing educational levels or programs of 
 16041  study upon their arrival in the United States. These students often use 
 16042  an admission letter and Form I-20 from a well-known school to increase 
 16043  their odds of obtaining a student visa and then immediately request a 
 16044  transfer to their intended school or program of study once they have 
 16045  gained admission to the United States. Some of the most egregious 
 16046  examples are those who apply to a 4-year university, which requires 
 16047  demonstration of sufficient English level skills for enrollment in 
 16048  classes through the passage of the Test of English as a Foreign 
 16049  Language test (commonly known as TOEFL), receive their visa based on 
 16050  their declared intention of attending a 4-year university, and then 
 16051  transfer to English language programs upon arrival. Other, more 
 16052  dangerous examples, include those foreign students who receive a visa 
 16053  based on their declared intention to study the humanities, but then 
 16054  transfer into sensitive programs such as nuclear science. A handful of 
 16055  those have been arrested for spying for China.\314\ The existing 
 16056  regulations are vulnerable to exploitation by aliens who threaten U.S. 
 16057  national security. This rule is designed to reduce this vulnerability. 
 16058  Since 2020, there have been over 13,000 F-1 students who transferred 
 16059  before the start of classes or within their first term, including over 
 16060  4,400 students transferring from a higher education to ELT program of 
 16061  study within their first
 16062  
 16063  [[Page 45104]]
 16064  
 16065  term or session of a program of study.\315\ The number of F-1 students 
 16066  who changed their educational levels within the first 60 days of their 
 16067  program is close to 8,400.\316\ While the number of students 
 16068  transferring or changing educational levels represents a small 
 16069  percentage of the total F-1 student population, these transfers are 
 16070  often promoted by third-party recruiters and other for-profit entities 
 16071  to allow aliens to use the student visa process to mask their intent in 
 16072  the United States or circumvent F-1 restrictions.\317\ In addition, 
 16073  school officials are often burdened with the administrative costs of 
 16074  processing SEVIS transfer requests from F-1 students who misrepresented 
 16075  their intentions of studying at their institution.
 16076  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16077  
 16078      \314\ See CNN Politics, Chinese Engineer Sentenced to 8 years in 
 16079  US Prison for Spying, supra note 82, and Senate Select Committee on 
 16080  Intelligence Hearing (Feb. 13, 2018), supra note 82.
 16081      \315\ See SEVIS Data on Initial Transfers and Change of 
 16082  Education Counts (Mar. 31, 2025).
 16083      \316\ Id.
 16084      \317\ On May 29, 2020, President Trump signed a Presidential 
 16085  Proclamation to suspend the entry as nonimmigrants of certain 
 16086  students and researchers from the PRC. See Suspension of Entry as 
 16087  Nonimmigrants of Certain Students and Researchers from the People's 
 16088  Republic of China, Proc. No. 10043, 85 FR 34353 (Jun. 4, 2020). 
 16089  Since this proclamation, students often circumvent enforcement of 
 16090  this proclamation by applying to a permissible program of study to 
 16091  obtain a student visa and admission to the United States and then 
 16092  transferring or changing their program of study to engage in 
 16093  studies, research, and other activities that are prohibited. This is 
 16094  also a tactic used by international and third-party recruiters. See 
 16095  Inside Higher Ed., Gaming the Student Visa System (Jan. 12, 2024), 
 16096  https://www.insidehighered.com/news/global/international-students-us/2024/01/12/international-admission-offices-plagued-fraud-and.
 16097  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16098  
 16099      While there may be legitimate cases of students who wish to change 
 16100  their educational objective to gain knowledge at a lower or the same 
 16101  educational level, the traditional path of study typically progresses 
 16102  from a lower educational program to a higher one. The existing 
 16103  regulations present a model consistent with the majority of bona fide 
 16104  students who follow this traditional trajectory. The term ``full course 
 16105  of study'' as defined in the existing regulations requires that the 
 16106  program ``lead to the attainment of a specific educational or 
 16107  professional objective.'' \318\ Repeated changes to a program of study 
 16108  either within the same educational level or to move to a lower level, 
 16109  as well as immediate changes to a program of study upon initial entry 
 16110  into the United States, are not consistent with attainment of such an 
 16111  educational or professional objective. This understanding was reflected 
 16112  in the preamble to a 1986 rulemaking proposing changes to the F 
 16113  regulations, which stated: ``The proposed regulation. . .places 
 16114  limitations on the length of time a student may remain in any one level 
 16115  of study. Thus, the Service has eliminated applications for [EOS] for 
 16116  students who are progressing from one educational level to another but 
 16117  has placed a control over students who, for an inordinate length of 
 16118  time, remain in one level of study.'' \319\ But, by 1991, INS 
 16119  eliminated all EOS applications and began to rely on DSO's to make the 
 16120  decision on whether educational progress was being made. In the decades 
 16121  that have followed, it has become clear that this has enabled thousands 
 16122  to stay here for decades by switching programs and not making any 
 16123  upward progress.\320\
 16124  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16125  
 16126      \318\ 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i).
 16127      \319\ Nonimmigrant Classes; Change of Nonimmigrant 
 16128  Classification, 51 FR 27867 (Aug. 4, 1986).
 16129      \320\ By reviewing SEVIS data as of Apr. 6, 2025, DHS has 
 16130  identified 2,137 aliens who first entered as F-1 students between 
 16131  2000 and 2010 and remain in active F-1 status today.
 16132  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16133  
 16134      Consistent with the NPRM, DHS is restricting school transfers and 
 16135  changes of educational objectives within a student's first academic 
 16136  year of a program of study, unless an exception is authorized by SEVP, 
 16137  and prohibiting F-1 students in a graduate level program of study from 
 16138  changing educational objectives at any point during their program of 
 16139  study. F-1 students in a graduate level program of study are also 
 16140  prohibited from transferring, but the proposed regulatory text has been 
 16141  amended to allow SEVP to authorize an exception to this prohibition due 
 16142  to extenuating circumstances. ``Educational objectives'' refers to an 
 16143  F-1 student's educational level or major. See new 8 CFR 
 16144  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) and new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i). DHS believes these 
 16145  changes will accommodate the legitimate academic activities of bona 
 16146  fide students, such as a desire to pursue a different field of study or 
 16147  more specialized studies in their current field. These changes will 
 16148  also provide SEVP with flexibility to grant exceptions for extenuating 
 16149  circumstances. For example, an exception may be appropriate when a 
 16150  school closes or when a school has a prolonged inability to hold in-
 16151  person classes due to a natural disaster or other causes. DHS has also 
 16152  clarified in the final rule that extenuating circumstances include 
 16153  students needing to change schools to complete elementary or secondary 
 16154  education.
 16155      In addition, an alien who has completed a program as an F-1 
 16156  nonimmigrant at one educational level will be unable to maintain F-1 
 16157  status, depart and be admitted in F-1 status, or otherwise obtain F-1 
 16158  status (e.g., via a change of status) through a program at the same 
 16159  educational level or a lower educational level. See new 8 CFR 
 16160  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C). However, an F-1 student who has completed a program 
 16161  in the United States at one educational level and is beginning a new 
 16162  program at a higher educational level will be considered to be 
 16163  maintaining F-1 status if they otherwise comply with requirements under 
 16164  8 CFR 214.2(f). See new 8 CFR 214.2 (f)(5)(ii)(B). These provisions 
 16165  were retained from the NPRM to the final rule. They will be applied 
 16166  prospectively. Any programs completed prior to the effective date of 
 16167  the rule will not be counted towards the limits.\321\
 16168  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16169  
 16170      \321\ For example, an F-1 student who completed a master's 
 16171  degree prior to the effective date of the rule would be eligible to 
 16172  enroll in and be admitted for the completion of another master's 
 16173  degree. Any programs completed after the effective date of the rule 
 16174  would be counted towards the new limits of this rule.
 16175  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16176  
 16177      DHS believes that it is reasonable for a student to progress to a 
 16178  higher educational level rather than continue at the same level or 
 16179  pursue a lower level of education, as that is the traditional 
 16180  trajectory in the pursuit of higher education. Movement within the same 
 16181  level after completion of a program to a lower educational level raises 
 16182  concerns regarding whether the F-1 student is a bona fide student who 
 16183  intends to temporarily and solely pursue a full course of study rather 
 16184  than pursuing different degrees as a de facto way to prolong their stay 
 16185  in the United States.
 16186      If an F-1 student who has completed their first academic year of a 
 16187  program of study seeks to change educational objectives and this change 
 16188  would require an EOS, the alien would then apply for EOS using the form 
 16189  designated by USCIS, paying the required fee and following all form 
 16190  instructions, including submitting any biometrics required by 8 CFR 
 16191  103.16. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(D).
 16192      DHS recognized that these changes might require updates to SEVIS 
 16193  and other systems. Because the timeframe for those updates is not fixed 
 16194  and there could be technical issues regarding implementation, DHS is 
 16195  including a provision whereby DHS may delay or suspend implementation, 
 16196  in its discretion, if it determines that the change in educational 
 16197  level limitation is inoperable for any reason. The need for this 
 16198  provision is not indefinite and therefore DHS has added language in the 
 16199  regulatory text to clarify that this provision can be used for up to 
 16200  two years from the effective date of the rule (i.e., September 14, 
 16201  2028). See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E). If DHS delays or suspends the 
 16202  provisions in this section governing the change in educational 
 16203  objectives, DHS will make an
 16204  
 16205  [[Page 45105]]
 16206  
 16207  announcement of the delay or suspension by notice in the Federal 
 16208  Register and to the academic community through SEVP's various 
 16209  communication channels, including ICE.gov/sevis, Study in the States 
 16210  (https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov), and SEVIS Broadcast Message. DHS 
 16211  will also announce the implementation dates of the change in degree 
 16212  level provision through SEVP's communication channels (ICE.gov/sevis, 
 16213  Study in the States, and SEVIS Broadcast Message) at least 30 calendar 
 16214  days in advance.
 16215      Additionally, DHS is retaining the term ``educational'' with 
 16216  respect to a change in level as DHS believes it accurately reflects 
 16217  current academic models. Specifically, ``educational'' captures 
 16218  programs for non-degree students, whereas using a term such as 
 16219  ``degree'' may not. For example, an F-1 student currently will not 
 16220  qualify for additional post-completion OPT if he or she changes to a 
 16221  non-degree certificate program, given that the certificate program is 
 16222  not a ``higher educational level.'' Similarly, certificate programs for 
 16223  professional advancement are typically not considered to be a ``higher 
 16224  educational level'' allowing students to qualify for additional post-
 16225  completion OPT.
 16226      DHS believes these changes will encourage F-1 students to complete 
 16227  the programs of study for which they were admitted to the United States 
 16228  and to only pursue additional programs of study that demonstrate an 
 16229  upward progression in degree levels, which is expected from a qualified 
 16230  bona fide student who is coming to the United States temporarily and 
 16231  solely to pursue a course of study. DHS believes that this restriction 
 16232  will not significantly impact the choice of bona fide students who come 
 16233  to the United States temporarily to complete a full course of study. 
 16234  The F-1 program, with its statutory requirement that an alien be a bona 
 16235  fide student who seeks to enter the United States temporarily and 
 16236  solely for the purpose of pursuing a full course of study at the school 
 16237  listed on his or her Form I-20 or successor form, should not be used by 
 16238  aliens wishing to remain in the United States indefinitely. These 
 16239  changes will better ensure that this statutory intent is fulfilled 
 16240  without hindering the options presented to bona fide students seeking 
 16241  study at higher educational levels and thus create a balanced solution 
 16242  to this issue.
 16243  3. Preparation for Departure
 16244      DHS retains its proposal from the NPRM to change the departure 
 16245  period for F nonimmigrants from 60 to 30 days. See new 8 CFR 
 16246  214.2(f)(5)(v). DHS received comments on this change, and those 
 16247  comments are discussed elsewhere in this preamble. DHS made this change
